item.title: EYE NEWSFLASH: Greens propose sweeping rent caps as agents warn of landlord exodus
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The Green Party has proposed radical reforms to the private rental sector, including strict rent caps and the abolition of leasehold tenure. The proposals, announced at their recent conference, have drawn both support from tenant groups and warnings from property industry bodies about potential unintended consequences.

Green Party's rental market proposals

Under the Green Party's plans, annual rent increases would be limited to either inflation, wage growth or 2% — whichever is lowest — for a three-year period. The policy aims to protect tenants from sudden rent hikes and prevent landlords from using excessive increases to force occupants out of properties.

Party leader Zack Polanski criticised current government policies as inadequate, arguing that stronger tenant protections are needed. The Greens' proposals go beyond Labour's rental reform plans, with additional measures including:

  • A national fair rents guarantee to maintain long-term affordability
  • The complete abolition of the leasehold system
  • Substantial increases in council housebuilding programmes

Industry concerns about rent controls

Propertymark, the professional body for estate agents, has raised significant concerns about the potential impact of rent controls. The organisation warns that such measures could accelerate the current trend of landlords leaving the market, potentially exacerbating the housing shortage.

Timothy Douglas of Propertymark highlighted the Scottish experience, where temporary rent caps reportedly led to some landlords selling properties or increasing rents between tenancies. He argued that policymakers should focus instead on increasing housing supply and encouraging responsible investment in the private rental sector.

International evidence suggests that rent controls can have several unintended consequences:

  • Reduced investment in rental properties
  • Deterioration in housing quality as maintenance budgets shrink
  • Landlords exiting the market entirely
  • Potential increase in rents between tenancies to compensate for capped increases

While tenant affordability remains a pressing issue, industry experts caution that rent controls alone cannot solve the fundamental problem of housing undersupply. Propertymark suggests that any reforms must balance immediate renter protections with long-term strategies to expand available housing stock.

As debates around rental reform continue, homeowners and landlords may wish to monitor policy developments that could affect both the rental market and broader property sector in coming years.

item.title: UK rents surge as regional divide widens
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

UK rents have climbed by nearly 5% over the past year, with tenants now paying an average of £1,581 per month compared to £1,507 in September 2022. However, the latest data highlights a growing disparity between regional rental markets, with some areas experiencing significant increases while others show signs of stagnation or decline. This trend underscores the challenges faced by renters across the country, particularly in regions where demand continues to outstrip supply.

Regional variations in rental growth

The North East has emerged as the region with the strongest rental growth, with prices soaring by 13.9% over the past year. Tenants in this area now pay an average of £1,000 per month, up from £878 in 2022. Wales followed closely behind with a 7.4% increase, bringing average rents to £994. Yorkshire and the Humber and the North West also saw notable rises, with growth rates of 6.9% and 6.1% respectively.

Meanwhile, Greater London recorded a 4.4% increase, pushing average rents to £2,306 per month. The South East experienced more modest growth at 3.1%, while the East of England became the only region to see a decline, with rents falling by 0.4% to £1,375. The East Midlands also showed signs of slowing growth, with rents increasing by just 1.8% over the year.

Monthly trends and void periods

On a monthly basis, the North East once again led the way, with rents rising by 5.6% between August and September. The North West and South West also saw increases of 3.1% and 2.5% respectively. Yorkshire and the Humber was the only region to record a slight monthly decline, although the reduction was minimal.

The average rental void period across the UK shortened slightly, dropping from 21 days in August to 20 days in September. The North East recorded the shortest voids, averaging just 11 days between tenancies, while Yorkshire and the Humber had the longest at 29 days.

Outlook for rental inflation

Despite the continued rise in rents, there are indications that the pace of rental inflation may be moderating in certain areas. William Reeve, chief executive of Goodlord, noted that while rental averages continue to outstrip inflation year-on-year, the overall rate of growth appears to be easing. This could offer some relief to tenants, though the ongoing supply and demand pressures mean rental affordability remains a concern for many.

For those navigating the rental market, staying informed about regional trends and understanding local dynamics could help in making more informed decisions. Renters might also consider exploring areas with slower growth or negotiating rental terms to manage costs effectively.

item.title: Letting agents and landlords put on alert as council steps up HMO crackdown
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Landlords and letting agents in Barnet are being urged to review their licensing obligations as the council intensifies its crackdown on unlicensed Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs). Recent enforcement efforts have seen Barnet Council conduct targeted evening inspections, with legal investigations now underway for 22 properties suspected of breaching licensing rules.

Understanding HMO Licensing Requirements

In Barnet, HMOs that meet specific criteria must hold the appropriate licence. The council maintains a public register of licensed properties, making it easier for landlords and agents to verify compliance. Beyond licensing, landlords are also required to ensure their properties meet stringent management and safety standards.

Failure to adhere to these regulations can lead to significant financial penalties. Barnet Council has already issued fines totalling £187,000 this year for HMO-related offences, with individual penalties reaching up to £40,000. This highlights the importance of ensuring properties are properly licensed and managed.

Increased Enforcement Measures

The recent evening inspections are part of a broader enforcement strategy. During the first operation, council officers visited 76 properties, identifying numerous cases of potential non-compliance. These inspections are not a one-off initiative; Barnet Council has confirmed plans to continue targeted operations across the borough over the next 12 months.

Letting and managing agents are particularly encouraged to verify the licensing status of properties under their supervision. Compliance should be reviewed regularly, especially when taking on new properties or managing existing portfolios. This proactive approach can help avoid costly penalties and legal issues.

Steps for Landlords and Agents

For landlords and agents operating in Barnet, there are several steps to ensure compliance:

  • Check whether your property requires an HMO licence using the council’s public register.
  • Ensure all licensing, management, and safety requirements are met.
  • Regularly review compliance, particularly when changes are made to the property or tenancy agreements.

By staying informed and proactive, landlords and agents can avoid the substantial penalties associated with licensing breaches.

Barnet Council’s heightened enforcement efforts underscore the importance of adhering to HMO regulations. With ongoing inspections and significant fines for non-compliance, landlords and agents are advised to act swiftly to ensure their properties meet all legal requirements.

item.title: Landlord Law Newsround #456
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

October has brought significant changes for UK landlords, with new right-to-rent rules taking effect alongside growing concerns about property management challenges. Recent surveys suggest landlords face mounting compliance pressures, while market data reveals rising tenant financial difficulties and longer void periods between tenancies.

Growing pressures for self-managing landlords

New research highlights the increasing difficulties facing landlords who manage properties themselves. A survey by property management firm Rushbrook found 74% of self-managing landlords report the task has become more challenging compared to three years ago. Maintenance and repairs remain the most time-consuming aspect for 52% of respondents, whilst compliance issues rank as the most stressful element.

The Renters' Reform Bill's impending changes, alongside existing regulatory requirements, have prompted many landlords to reconsider self-management. However, industry experts caution that appointing a letting agent doesn't automatically transfer legal responsibilities. Paul Endacott of 1st Avenue notes: "The biggest risk facing landlords today may be assuming someone else manages compliance when, legally, the responsibility ultimately rests with the property owner."

Tenant referencing takes on greater importance

Registry Trust data shows an 11.6% annual increase in County Court Judgments (CCJs) against consumers, with 6% of UK adults now having at least one adverse credit marker. This trend means landlords are increasingly likely to encounter prospective tenants with financial difficulties.

Allison Thompson, Chief Lettings Officer at Leaders, observes that landlords are becoming more thorough with referencing checks: "Most tenants still pass referencing processes, but with restrictions on taking rent in advance, robust referencing has become an essential tool for risk management." Industry reports indicate one in ten landlords have significantly tightened their tenant selection criteria in recent months.

Void periods lengthen as market shifts

The average void period between tenancies has extended to over three weeks across many UK regions. This extension reflects both seasonal patterns and broader market adjustments following recent legislative changes. Landlords may wish to factor these potential void periods into their financial planning, particularly when considering property investments or portfolio expansions.

For those navigating these challenges, specialist services like Landlord Law provide compliance guidance, whilst property management firms offer varying levels of support. With the rental market undergoing significant transformation, staying informed remains crucial for landlords at all experience levels.

item.title: Letting agent fined for breaching Renters’ Rights Act
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

A letting agent in Chesterfield has been fined over £8,600 for breaching regulations under the Renters’ Rights Act 2025. The agent issued a prohibited fixed-term tenancy agreement and instructed tenants to vacate the property after they raised concerns about its condition. Chesterfield Borough Council imposed the penalties following an investigation into the agent’s conduct, highlighting the importance of compliance with the new legislation.

Details of the Case

The case arose when tenants reported issues with their rented property shortly after moving in. Investigators found that the agent had issued a six-month fixed-term tenancy agreement, which is prohibited under the Renters’ Rights Act 2025. Additionally, the agent told the tenants to leave when they indicated they would lodge a formal complaint. The tenants subsequently moved to alternative accommodation owned by another landlord, whose identity remains undisclosed.

The council imposed two financial penalties totalling £8,652, though the agent paid a reduced amount of £7,354.20 after settling within the specified timeframe. Alongside the fines, the council issued an improvement notice requiring the property to meet housing standards. This case serves as a stark reminder to letting agents and landlords of their obligations under the new legislation.

Council’s Warning to Letting Agents

Chesterfield Borough Council has emphasised the importance of compliance with the Renters’ Rights Act. Councillor Jean Innes, the council’s cabinet member for housing, stated that the authority had engaged with local landlords and letting agents prior to the legislation’s implementation to ensure they understood the changes. She added, “We are committed to putting our communities first and making sure renters have the protection they need. This case demonstrates that we will take action where landlords and agents fail to comply with their duties.”

The council hopes this case will serve as a reminder to letting agents across Chesterfield to fully understand the recent changes to the law and their responsibilities. The Renters’ Rights Act, which came into force on 1 May 2026, aims to provide greater protection for tenants and ensure fair treatment in the rental market.

What This Means for Landlords and Agents

Landlords and letting agents may wish to review their practices to ensure compliance with the Renters’ Rights Act. Key areas to focus on include avoiding prohibited tenancy agreements and addressing tenant concerns promptly and fairly. Failure to comply could result in significant financial penalties and damage to reputation.

Tenants, on the other hand, can take reassurance from the council’s proactive approach to enforcing the legislation. Those facing issues with their rental property may consider contacting their local authority for support and guidance.

This case underscores the importance of understanding and adhering to housing legislation, benefiting both tenants and landlords in the long term.

item.title: Propertymark calls for landlord licensing schemes to be abolished
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Propertymark, a leading trade body for the property sector, has called for the abolition of discretionary landlord licensing schemes across England. The organisation argues that these local schemes, which require landlords to obtain licences to operate, impose unnecessary costs and administrative burdens. With the introduction of the national Private Rented Sector (PRS) Database, Propertymark believes there is an opportunity to streamline regulation and improve enforcement without the need for local licensing systems.

The case against local licensing schemes

In a recent position paper titled The Effectiveness of Local Authority Landlord Licensing Schemes, Propertymark questioned whether selective and additional licensing schemes provide sufficient benefits to justify their costs. The organisation highlighted that licensing fees can exceed £1,000 per property in some areas, with additional licensing schemes costing even more. For landlords managing larger portfolios, these charges can quickly escalate into tens of thousands of pounds.

Propertymark also raised concerns about the effectiveness of enforcement by local authorities. Research indicates that around two-thirds of English councils had not prosecuted a landlord in the three years leading up to the study, despite receiving an estimated 300,000 complaints annually about property conditions. Furthermore, over 84% of councils reported difficulties recruiting environmental health professionals, which could hinder their ability to enforce housing standards effectively.

Proposals for reform

Propertymark has proposed several reforms to improve the current system. The trade body advocates for greater transparency regarding how councils spend licensing income, suggesting that fees should be directly linked to inspections and enforcement efforts. Additionally, it has called for a national cap on administration costs, limiting them to 20% of licensing fees.

Tim Thomas, Propertymark’s Senior Policy and Campaigns Officer, emphasised the need for clarity and enforcement. “Landlords should be able to see a clear connection between the fees they pay and the improvements being delivered in their local housing market,” he said. “The priority must be enforcement. A licensing system should not become an end in itself, particularly where councils already have extensive powers to identify and act against unsafe or poorly managed housing.”

The national PRS database

The introduction of the national PRS Database, known as the Register Your Rental Property service, is seen as a potential replacement for local licensing schemes. The first phase of the database is scheduled to launch on 15 December 2026, beginning in the West Midlands before rolling out across England over the following 12 months. Once fully operational, the database will require all landlords actively letting properties in England to register their details.

Propertymark believes the national database could simplify regulation, reduce costs for landlords, and improve enforcement by providing a centralised system for monitoring compliance. This shift could mark a significant step towards a more efficient and transparent private rental sector.

As the property sector awaits the implementation of the PRS Database, Propertymark’s proposals have sparked debate about the future of landlord licensing and the best ways to ensure safe and well-managed rental properties across England.

item.title: House prices hit decade-high affordability – but buyers face a sting in the tail
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

New data suggests UK housing affordability has reached its most favourable level in nearly a decade, though rising mortgage rates mean many buyers continue to face financial pressures. According to recent analysis, the average property now costs 7.3 times annual earnings, down from 7.6 times last year – marking the lowest house price-to-income ratio since 2015.

Wage growth outpaces property prices

The improved affordability ratio stems from a widening gap between earnings and house price growth. Over the past year, average salaries increased by 4.5% to £40,790, while property values rose just 0.5% to £299,131. First-time buyers have seen some relief too, with their price-to-earnings ratio falling from 6.1 to 5.9 as prices crept up by only 0.3%.

However, these headline figures don't tell the full story. Despite improved affordability ratios, homeowners now face higher monthly repayments due to elevated mortgage rates. The average monthly mortgage payment has increased by £57 over the past year, reaching £1,157.

Regional variations in affordability

The most significant improvements occurred in England's priciest housing markets. The South East saw its ratio drop from 9.7 to 9.1, while London's fell from 10.9 to 10.3. Eastern England and the South West also recorded notable declines to 8.2 and 7.7 respectively. Nevertheless, London and the South East remain the nation's least affordable regions.

Other areas showed more modest changes:

  • North East: 5.1 to 5.0
  • Scotland: Remained steady at 5.3
  • North West: 6.5 to 6.3
  • Yorkshire and the Humber: 6.0 to 5.8

Northern Ireland proved the exception, with house prices rising 7.4% – nearly double the 3.7% wage growth – pushing its ratio up from 5.8 to 6.0.

Ongoing challenges for buyers

While the figures suggest some positive movement, industry experts caution that affordability pressures persist. Mortgage rates remain substantially higher than recent historic lows, and saving for deposits continues to challenge first-time buyers in particular.

Some borrowers might consider exploring mortgage products designed for those with smaller deposits, though these won't suit every situation. As always, prospective buyers may wish to seek independent financial advice to understand their full range of options in the current market.

For those considering a property purchase, weighing both house price affordability and ongoing mortgage costs remains crucial when assessing what's financially manageable in the long term.

Key leadership changes are underway in the UK property sector, with notable appointments and transitions shaping the future of several prominent estate agency brands. New Leadership at Lomond’s Southern Region

Lomond has announced the appointment of Neil McGimpsey as chief revenue officer for its southern region. McGimpsey, who previously served as Lomond’s chief operating officer, will now oversee the performance and growth of the group’s southern agency brands, including Charters, Miles & Barr, Prospect, and Ocean. His extensive experience in the property sector, including 15 years in senior roles at Foxtons and a stint as chief executive of Druce & Co, positions him as a strong candidate to drive Lomond’s regional strategy forward.

McGimpsey’s appointment follows the departure of Rob Mott, founder of Charters, who is stepping down after 18 years. Lomond’s decision to appoint McGimpsey aligns with its broader strategy to strengthen its regional management structure. item.title: London rental demand rebounds as supply falls 10%
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

London’s rental market has experienced a notable resurgence in recent weeks, with tenant demand overtaking last year’s figures despite dwindling property availability. According to Rightmove’s latest data, rental enquiries in the capital were 7% higher in September 2026 compared to the same period in 2025 – marking a clear reversal of the downward trend observed earlier in the year.

Shifting dynamics in London’s rental market

Rightmove’s Daily Demand Tracker reveals that tenant enquiries first surpassed 2025 levels on 7th September and have remained consistently higher since. This recovery stands in stark contrast to the broader national picture, where overall rental demand across Great Britain sits 2% lower year-on-year. The North East represents the only other region showing growth, albeit at a modest 1%.

The capital’s rental rebound coincides with shrinking property supply, with available homes to let now 10% fewer than twelve months ago. This contrasts with the marginal 0.4% increase in rental stock observed across Great Britain as a whole. As competition intensifies, average advertised rents in London have climbed to £2,763 per month – a 3.1% annual increase compared to the national average rise of 2.4% to £1,578.

Smaller properties driving demand

The resurgence appears particularly pronounced among smaller properties, with studios and one-bedroom homes leading the charge. Enquiries for these compact dwellings have surged by 10% in London compared to a 4% national increase. The average advertised rent for such properties in the capital now stands at £1,904 monthly, significantly above the £1,150 national equivalent for similar-sized homes.

While larger properties have also seen demand growth, the pace remains more measured. Two-bedroom homes recorded a 6% increase in enquiries, with three-bedroom properties attracting 2.5% more interest than last year. This contrasts sharply with national trends where demand for two and three-bedroom properties has fallen by 4% and 6% respectively.

Potential factors behind the rebound

Market analysts suggest several factors may be contributing to London’s rental market recovery. Colleen Babcock, Rightmove’s property expert, notes: “Affordability pressures and elevated mortgage rates might be encouraging some would-be first-time buyers to extend their time in rented accommodation. The challenge of saving for deposits and bridging affordability gaps appears particularly acute in the capital.”

Prospective homeowners facing these financial hurdles might consider reviewing their savings strategies or exploring government schemes designed to support first-time buyers. Meanwhile, landlords with available properties could find themselves in a stronger negotiating position as demand outpaces supply in certain London postcodes.

As autumn progresses, industry observers will be watching closely to see whether London’s rental market maintains its upward trajectory or if seasonal patterns bring new shifts to the capital’s property landscape.

item.title: SpareRoom launches celebrity podcast exploring what ‘home’ really means
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The meaning of "home" goes beyond bricks and mortar, as explored in SpareRoom's new podcast series featuring well-known personalities sharing their personal housing stories. Home Again, launched on 29 September, shifts the conversation from property prices to emotional connections with living spaces, with guests including broadcaster Stacey Dooley, comedian Guz Khan, and rugby player Meg Jones.

Celebrity perspectives on meaningful homes

Unlike typical property discussions focusing on market trends, this podcast invites guests to reflect on three significant homes that shaped their lives. Dooley shares how her global travels influenced her eventual choice of a long-term home, while Khan recounts the unexpected discovery in his family home. The series also touches on relatable experiences – from Matt Edmondson's flatsharing stories to Jones' use of her home as a social hub.

SpareRoom's communications director Matt Hutchinson, who co-hosts alongside social media specialist Ella Chisholm, explains: "We wanted to move beyond viewing housing purely as accommodation. Homes profoundly affect our wellbeing and identity, yet these emotional aspects often get overlooked in national housing debates."

Redefining housing conversations

The twelve-episode series aims to celebrate diverse interpretations of home. Chisholm notes: "While everyone understands the concept of home, each person's experience is deeply personal. Our guests' stories range from nostalgic to brutally honest – perhaps because home is where we're most authentic."

For homeowners and renters alike, the podcast offers a refreshing alternative to financial-focused property content. The production comes from SpareRoom, the UK's leading flatshare site, though it deliberately avoids rental market discussions to explore broader themes of belonging and personal growth through living spaces.

New episodes release weekly on major platforms, presenting a different perspective on how our surroundings influence life journeys – from career choices to personal relationships.

item.title: Fifty not out: RICS Red Book celebrates half a century
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS) is celebrating the 50th anniversary of its Red Book this year – the globally recognised valuation standard that shapes property assessments across residential, commercial and other asset markets. Since its introduction in 1976, the framework has expanded from UK-specific guidance to an international benchmark relied upon by lenders, investors and property professionals worldwide.

The origins and evolution of valuation standards

The Red Book emerged from financial turbulence in the early 1970s property market, where inconsistent valuation methods contributed to market instability. Developed jointly with the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales, the first edition established much-needed consistency in asset assessments. Today, RICS estimates the standards underpin valuations for assets worth £10 trillion in the UK alone.

Over five decades, the framework has grown to encompass professional ethics, transparency requirements and competency standards alongside valuation methodologies. Updated biennially through global consultation, the guidance now supports mortgage lending decisions, financial reporting and major property transactions across 160 countries, with translations available in seven languages.

Adapting to modern property challenges

As RICS marks this milestone, attention turns to how valuation standards must evolve to address emerging technologies and market trends. The institution highlights artificial intelligence, big data analytics and sustainability considerations as key factors reshaping modern property assessments.

Charlotte Neal, RICS Director of Professional Practice and Research, notes: "While consistency remains the Red Book's foundation, its true value lies in fostering credibility during economic uncertainty. When stakeholders rely on valuations for critical financial decisions, these standards provide the necessary framework for professional judgement."

The anniversary comes as valuation professionals navigate new asset classes, climate-related disclosures and technological disruption. RICS confirms the Red Book will continue adapting to these changes while maintaining core principles of integrity, objectivity and professional competence that have defined it for half a century.

For homeowners and mortgage borrowers, these evolving standards help ensure property valuations reflect genuine market conditions – a crucial factor when securing financing or making investment decisions. As the property landscape transforms, these professional guidelines aim to maintain trust in valuation processes across all market conditions.

item.title: Property tax revenues hit new high as buyers face mounting costs
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Scottish property tax revenues have surged to unprecedented levels, raising concerns about the impact of rising transaction costs on buyers and investors. According to analysis by DJ Alexander, Land and Buildings Transaction Tax (LBTT) generated £758.9 million in the 12 months to August 2026, marking a 12.1% increase compared to the previous year. This growth highlights the escalating financial burden on those entering the Scottish property market.

Record-Breaking LBTT Revenues

Residential LBTT, excluding the Additional Dwelling Supplement (ADS), accounted for £52.3 million in August 2026 alone—the highest August figure on record and a 3% rise compared to August 2025. Over the same 12-month period, ADS generated £228.1 million, representing a significant 25.1% increase year-on-year. This contributed to nearly 30% of total LBTT receipts.

However, recent monthly data suggests a slight cooling in the market. Gross ADS receipts in August 2026 dropped by 4% compared to the previous year, with the number of ADS declarations falling by 9% to 1,690. Despite this, the proportion of buyers falling outside LBTT tax bands has decreased sharply since its introduction. In 2015, 52.4% of buyers paid no LBTT, but by August 2026, this figure had fallen to 30.9%.

Impact on Buyers and Investors

David Alexander, chief executive of DJ Alexander Scotland, has cautioned that rising transaction costs could deter buyers and investors. He noted that while LBTT revenues remain high, there is a growing risk that buyers may delay or abandon their property purchases due to affordability concerns. Investors, in particular, might seek opportunities in less heavily taxed regions, such as the rest of the UK or overseas.

Alexander also highlighted the potential impact on existing homeowners. High transaction costs could discourage those in larger properties from moving, creating a ripple effect across the housing market. This stagnation could limit options for buyers in smaller homes, further complicating the property landscape.

Long-Term Implications for the Market

The sustained increase in LBTT revenues underscores the financial pressures facing both buyers and sellers in Scotland. Whilst the tax has proven lucrative for the government, there is a growing debate about its long-term effects on housing activity. A highly taxed market risks discouraging new entrants and stifling mobility within the property sector.

Borrowers and investors might consider these factors when planning their property purchases, particularly in light of the additional costs associated with LBTT and ADS. Staying informed about market trends and tax implications could help individuals make more informed decisions.

As the Scottish property market continues to evolve, the balance between generating tax revenue and maintaining affordability remains a critical issue. Homeowners and buyers may wish to carefully evaluate their options in this increasingly complex environment.

item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The Landlord Law Blog provided a wealth of insights for property investors and landlords throughout September, covering everything from tribunal preparation to legislative updates. For those seeking to stay informed on the latest housing sector developments, the month's roundup offered several key takeaways.

Preparing for Rent Tribunals and Compliance Matters

The blog emphasised the importance of thorough preparation when facing rent tribunals, highlighting that last-minute documentation or attempts to cut corners could prove detrimental. Landlords might consider ensuring all paperwork is complete and organised well in advance of any hearings.

Another key piece focused on improvement notices, outlining the potential consequences of non-compliance. Property owners receiving such notices may wish to address required improvements promptly to avoid escalating penalties or legal action.

Legislative Changes Affecting Landlords

September's coverage included analysis of new rules surrounding Section 8 possession claims following the abolition of Section 21 notices. The blog described these adjustments as creating a "deposit trap" that landlords should be aware of when pursuing possession cases.

Looking further ahead, the blog flagged upcoming changes to Right to Rent checks scheduled for October 2026. Whilst this deadline may seem distant, landlords with tenant turnover might consider familiarising themselves with the forthcoming requirements to ensure smooth transitions.

item.title: UK house price growth halves as property market loses momentum
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

UK house price growth slowed significantly in September, according to Nationwide’s latest House Price Index. Annual growth fell to 0.8%, halving from August’s figure of 1.6%, marking the weakest performance since December 2025. Month-on-month, prices dipped by 0.2%, reversing the previous month’s 0.2% increase. The average UK property price now stands at £274,251, down from £275,465 in August. This slowdown reflects ongoing economic uncertainty, inflationary pressures, and the impact of higher mortgage rates on the property market.

Economic pressures weigh on the market

Robert Gardner, Nationwide’s chief economist, highlighted the challenging economic backdrop as a key factor behind the subdued housing market activity. Geopolitical tensions, particularly in the Middle East, have pushed energy prices higher, fuelling inflation concerns. This has led to expectations of further Bank of England rate hikes, which in turn has kept mortgage rates elevated. Gardner noted that these factors have contributed to the cooling of house price growth.

Despite the slowdown, there are signs of improving affordability, with earnings rising faster than house prices. Gardner suggested that a recovery in housing market activity could be on the horizon if energy prices stabilise, consumer confidence strengthens, and mortgage rates ease. However, for now, the market remains under pressure, with buyers and sellers navigating a challenging landscape.

Regional disparities widen

Nationwide’s regional data for the third quarter reveals a stark North-South divide in the UK housing market. Eight of the 13 regions recorded annual house price growth below 1%, with four experiencing outright declines. Northern Ireland emerged as the strongest performer, with prices rising by 5.9% year-on-year, although this was a slowdown from 8.6% in the previous quarter. In England, the North West led the way with a 3.9% increase, followed by Scotland and the North of England, both recording growth of 3.3%.

In contrast, southern England saw a 0.1% annual decline in house prices. London was the only southern region to register growth, albeit a modest 0.4%, down from 1.6% in the previous quarter. East Anglia was the weakest-performing region, with prices falling by 0.7% year-on-year. The East Midlands, South West, and Outer Metropolitan regions also experienced declines of 0.5%, 0.3%, and 0.2% respectively. These figures underscore the growing divergence between the more resilient northern markets and the struggling southern regions.

As the UK property market continues to navigate economic uncertainty and higher mortgage costs, homeowners and prospective buyers may wish to monitor regional trends and market developments closely. With affordability improving in some areas and mortgage rates potentially easing in the future, there could be opportunities for those looking to enter the market or make a move.

item.title: Fresh figures reveal growing pressure on the housing market
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

UK Housing Market Shows Signs of Strain as Transactions Decline

Recent provisional figures from HMRC reveal a dip in UK residential property transactions during August, with higher borrowing costs and economic uncertainty continuing to impact market activity. Seasonally adjusted data shows 95,220 completions for the month - a 1% decrease from July and 2% lower than August 2025. The unadjusted figures present an even steeper decline, with 96,250 properties changing hands, marking an 11% monthly and 9% annual drop.

Mixed Picture Across Different Timeframes

The latest statistics indicate nearly 9,000 fewer residential sales completed this August compared to the same month last year. However, the financial year-to-date presents a more positive outlook, with unadjusted transactions between April and August reaching 486,950 - a notable increase from 442,790 during the equivalent 2025/26 period.

Industry experts caution that transaction data operates as a lagging indicator, typically reflecting market conditions from two to four months prior when offers were originally made. This means the August figures may not accurately represent the current state of play in the property market.

Market Observations From Industry Professionals

Jeremy Leaf, a north London estate agent and former RICS residential chairman, notes that transaction volumes provide a more comprehensive market health check than house prices alone, as they encompass both mortgaged and cash purchases. He observes: "While concerns about mortgage rate increases and inflation persist, we've noticed renewed enthusiasm to move following the summer holiday period."

Richard Donnell from Zoopla points to more recent sales data suggesting further weakening, with agreed sales currently 9% lower than earlier in the year when mortgage rates stood at 4%. He comments: "The housing market continues to face challenges as higher mortgage rates increase the overall cost of purchasing a home."

While transaction volumes have softened, the underlying demand for housing remains. Prospective buyers and sellers may wish to consider that properties are taking longer to transact in the current climate, with increased choice available across most price ranges. Those monitoring the market might find it helpful to track both transaction data and mortgage rate movements when planning their next property move.

item.title: The property market’s biggest challenge: Getting sales to completion
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The UK property market faces significant challenges in 2024, with transaction volumes forecast to drop by 4.4% compared to next year's projections. While reduced buyer demand plays a role, industry experts highlight an even greater concern: the growing delays between sale agreements and completion.

Increasing Completion Times Create Market Headaches

Recent data reveals the average time from sale agreed to completion now stands at 154 days - over five months. This represents a substantial increase compared to pre-pandemic norms, with 60.8% of transactions now taking more than six months from instruction versus just 36.1% in 2019. Furthermore, approximately 23% of agreed sales ultimately fall through, creating financial uncertainty for all parties involved.

These delays have real consequences for estate agents and homeowners alike. For agencies, prolonged transaction times impact cash flow and make accurate forecasting difficult. For buyers and sellers, extended waiting periods increase the risk of chains collapsing and deals failing to complete.

Strategies to Improve Transaction Efficiency

Industry specialists suggest several approaches to streamline the sales process:

  • Early preparation: Addressing searches, documentation and compliance checks immediately after instruction can prevent bottlenecks later in the process
  • Chain awareness: Understanding the full transaction chain helps identify potential pressure points before they cause delays
  • Proactive communication: Regular updates between all parties help maintain momentum and quickly resolve emerging issues

Some specialist firms report significantly better performance metrics, with average completion times of just over 100 days and fall-through rates as low as 9%. These figures demonstrate that faster, more reliable completions are achievable with the right approach.

The Financial Impact of Delayed Completions

From an agency perspective, an agreed sale only generates revenue upon completion. With nearly a quarter of transactions currently failing to reach this stage, the financial implications are considerable. Each collapsed sale represents lost income after significant investment in marketing and negotiation.

The hidden costs of lengthy transactions also deserve consideration. Extended case management requires continuous staff time for queries, problem-solving and coordination - resources that could be deployed more effectively elsewhere in the business.

As the market continues to navigate economic uncertainties, improving conversion rates and reducing completion times may prove crucial for agencies aiming to maintain profitability in a challenging environment.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Two notable appointments in the UK property sector have recently been announced, with industry professionals taking on key roles in Guernsey and Essex. These moves highlight the ongoing evolution of the property market and the importance of experienced leadership in driving growth and maintaining professional standards.

Savills Welcomes New Residential Sales Director in Guernsey

Savills has appointed James Starkey as its new residential sales director in Guernsey, marking a strategic move to strengthen its presence on the island. Starkey brings a wealth of experience, having spent a decade in the residential property sector. His career includes roles at Guernsey-based agencies Swoffers and Cooper Brouard, followed by a stint in London where he worked in the prime Mayfair and Marylebone markets. Most recently, he led Chestertons’ Richmond office.

Starkey’s return to Guernsey sees him joining a well-established team at Savills, including director Nick Paluch and sales associates Kelsey Gerrard, Megan Chipperfield, and Monique Search. Reflecting on his new role, Starkey said, “Whilst I enjoyed my time in London immensely, Guernsey has a way of drawing people back. This was a great opportunity that came at the right time both personally and professionally. I grew up on the island, so I know just what a wonderful place it is to call home.”

Tony Rowbotham, head of office at Savills Guernsey, emphasised the significance of Starkey’s appointment. “He brings a wealth of experience and enthusiasm to a core area of our business where we are looking to grow and increase our market share. His understanding of the Guernsey property market ensures the evolution and expansion of our team continues, enhancing the services we offer to our clients.”

Propertymark Appoints New Regional Executive for Essex

In Essex, Paul Buck, director of sales and lettings at Boydens, has been appointed as Propertymark’s regional executive for the county. This role, secured through a selection process, will see Buck serve a three-year term. His responsibilities include supporting Propertymark members with training, promoting professional standards, and providing guidance on regulatory and legislative changes. He will also represent Propertymark at conferences and industry events.

Buck expressed his enthusiasm for the role, stating, “Being a regional executive gives me an opportunity to work with all the members throughout Essex to ensure they are getting the most out of their membership and that we are all working to the high standards required by Propertymark. I’ll also be assisting members with training requirements and helping them navigate the latest industry developments.”

These appointments reflect the dynamic nature of the UK property sector, with experienced professionals stepping into key roles to drive growth, maintain standards, and support industry members. As the market continues to evolve, such leadership will be crucial in navigating challenges and seizing opportunities.

item.title: Your First Home to stimulate development but more help needed
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The government's new "Your First Home" scheme has been broadly welcomed by property experts as a positive step for first-time buyers, though industry voices caution that deeper supply-side reforms may be needed to truly address the UK's housing challenges.

Support for first-time buyers

The initiative aims to stimulate housing development by making homeownership more accessible, particularly for younger buyers struggling to save substantial deposits. Through a combination of discounted pricing and shared ownership options, the scheme could help thousands take their first step onto the property ladder.

Mortgage advisors note that the programme builds upon existing schemes like Help to Buy, but with some key differences:

  • More flexible eligibility criteria compared to previous initiatives
  • Potential for lower deposit requirements in certain developments
  • Options for shared equity with local authorities

Persistent supply challenges

While welcoming the demand-side support, housing analysts highlight that fundamental supply constraints continue to limit overall market accessibility. The Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS) suggests that without addressing planning bottlenecks and construction sector capacity, price pressures may persist even with increased first-time buyer support.

Key supply-side issues that could benefit from further attention include:

  • Streamlining the planning application process
  • Incentives for brownfield site development
  • Investment in construction skills training

For prospective homeowners, the current landscape suggests that while government schemes can provide valuable assistance, exploring all available mortgage products and seeking independent financial advice remain important steps in the homebuying journey.

item.title: Two-thirds of landlords will increase rents if taxes rise
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

A recent study has revealed that a significant proportion of landlords in the UK may raise rents if faced with increased taxation or additional costs. The findings suggest that potential tax changes could lead to higher rental prices, with landlords becoming more selective about their tenants in response to financial pressures.

Impact of Tax Changes on Rental Prices

The research highlights that nearly two-thirds of landlords would consider increasing rents to offset any rise in taxes or operational costs. This could have a direct impact on tenants, particularly those already struggling with affordability in the current rental market. Whilst landlords aim to maintain profitability, tenants may face added financial strain as a result.

For homeowners and investors, this underscores the importance of staying informed about potential tax reforms and their implications. Understanding how these changes might affect rental income and property management costs could help landlords prepare for future adjustments.

Selective Tenant Choices

In addition to raising rents, the study suggests that landlords might become more selective when choosing tenants. This could mean prioritising applicants with stable incomes, strong credit histories, or longer rental commitments. Whilst this approach may help landlords mitigate financial risks, it could also make it more challenging for some tenants to secure rental properties.

For tenants, this highlights the value of maintaining a solid financial profile and ensuring all necessary documentation is readily available when applying for rentals. Landlords, on the other hand, may wish to review their tenant selection criteria to balance financial security with fairness.

What Does This Mean for the Rental Market?

The potential for higher rents and stricter tenant selection could reshape the UK rental market. Tenants may need to budget more carefully, whilst landlords might explore strategies to manage costs without passing the full burden onto renters. Proactive communication between landlords and tenants could also play a key role in navigating these changes.

Ultimately, the findings serve as a reminder of the interconnected nature of taxation, property investment, and rental affordability. Both landlords and tenants may benefit from staying informed and seeking professional advice where necessary to adapt to evolving market conditions.

As the UK property market continues to evolve, understanding the potential impact of tax changes on rental prices and tenant selection remains crucial for all parties involved.

item.title: £170k renovation vs new build cost
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Homeowners considering whether to renovate an older property or purchase a new build may find recent research revealing the financial implications of both options particularly insightful. The study highlights how bringing period homes up to modern standards could cost upwards of £170,000 – a figure that warrants careful consideration against the price of a newly constructed property.

The true cost of upgrading older homes

Research indicates that comprehensive renovations to match contemporary living standards often involve substantial investment. Common upgrades include improving energy efficiency through better insulation, replacing outdated heating systems with modern alternatives, and updating electrical wiring to current safety regulations. Structural repairs, damp proofing, and replacing single-glazed windows with double or triple glazing can also contribute significantly to costs.

While period properties often boast desirable character features, many require extensive modernisation to meet today's expectations of comfort and functionality. The £170,000 figure represents a full-scale refurbishment rather than cosmetic improvements, highlighting how seemingly minor issues can accumulate into major expenses when updating older buildings.

New builds versus renovation projects

For buyers weighing their options, new build properties typically come with modern specifications as standard, including energy-efficient appliances, contemporary heating systems, and warranties that cover structural defects. These benefits might prove attractive compared to the unpredictable costs and timescales associated with major renovation work.

However, period properties often occupy more established locations and offer architectural charm that new developments might lack. Some homeowners might prefer investing in renovation projects to create their ideal home while preserving historical character, despite the potentially higher initial outlay.

Prospective buyers may wish to consider not just the purchase price, but the total cost of ownership when comparing properties. Mortgage options for renovation projects differ from standard purchase mortgages, with some lenders offering specialist products for substantial refurbishments.

Ultimately, the decision between renovation and new build depends on individual priorities, budget considerations, and appetite for project management. While new builds offer convenience, older properties provide unique opportunities to create bespoke living spaces – provided purchasers are prepared for the potential scale of investment required.
